chunks: Muhammad ibn Ja'far, from Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Abdullah ibn Dahir, from Al-Hasan ibn Yahya, from Qutham Abu Qatada Al-Harrani, from Abdullah ibn Yunus, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

A man named Hammam, who was a worshipper, ascetic, and diligent, stood before the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) while he was delivering a sermon. He said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, describe to us the description of the believer, as if we are looking at him.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'O Hammam, the believer is the shrewd, the intelligent. His joy is on his face and his sorrow is in his heart. He is the most expansive in chest and the most humble in self. He restrains from everything perishable and is present for everything good. He is not spiteful, nor envious, nor quick to argue, nor abusive, nor fault-finding, nor backbiter. He dislikes elevation (status) and dislikes fame. He is long-suffering, far from worry, frequent in silence, dignified, remembering, patient, grateful. Gloomy in his thoughts, joyful in his poverty. Easy-going in nature, soft in manner, firm in loyalty, little in causing harm, neither pretentious nor excessive.'

If he laughs, he does not burst out; if he is angry, he does not become reckless. His laughter is a smile, his questioning is for learning, and his reference is for understanding. His knowledge is abundant, his forbearance is great, and he is full of mercy. He is not stingy, nor hasty, nor weary, nor arrogant, nor unjust in his judgment, nor unfair in his knowledge. His self is harder than the slab, and his temperament is sweeter than honey. He is not greedy, nor panicky, nor violent, nor arrogant, nor pretentious, nor excessive. He is good in dispute, generous in reference, just when angry, and friendly when sought.

He does not jeopardize, nor expose, nor be compulsive. He is pure in affection, firm in covenant, complete in contract. He is affectionate, maintaining ties, forbearing, calm, little in extravagance. He is pleased with Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and opposes his desire. He is not harsh to those below him, nor does he engage in what does not concern him. He is a supporter of the Religion, a defender of the believers, a cave for the Muslims. Praise does not pierce his hearing, nor does greed pierce his heart, nor does play divert his judgment, nor does he reveal his knowledge to the ignorant.

He is a speaker, a worker, knowledgeable, prudent. Not vulgar, nor frivolous. Maintaining ties without force, generous without extravagance. Not treacherous, nor deceitful. He does not follow faults, nor is he unjust to a person. He is kind to creation, striving in the land, a helper for the weak, a rescuer for the distressed. He does not tear down a veil, nor uncover a secret. He is much afflicted but little in complaint.

If he sees good, he mentions it; if he sees evil, he covers it. He veils faults, preserves the unseen, dismisses stumbles, and forgives slips. He does not neglect advice, nor leave a flaw uncorrected. He is trustworthy, firm, pious, pure, honest, and agreeable. He accepts excuses, beautifies mention, thinks well of people, and accuses himself of faults.

He loves in Allah with understanding and knowledge, and cuts off in Allah with firmness and determination. Joy does not burst through him, nor does cheerfulness make him erratic. He is a reminder for the knowledgeable, a teacher for the ignorant. A disaster is not expected from him, nor an affliction feared. Every striving is more sincere in his presence than his own striving, and every self is more correct in his presence than his own self. He knows his fault, occupied with his sorrow, trusts no one but his Lord. He is a stranger, alone, dispossessed, sad.

He loves in Allah and strives in Allah to follow His pleasure, and does not take revenge for himself, nor befriends for the sake of his Lord's anger. He sits with the poor, is a friend of the truthful, supports the people of truth, aids the relative, is a father to the orphan, a husband to the widow, hopeful for the destitute. He is hoped for every abhorrence, relied upon for every difficulty.

Light and happy, not frowning, not sly. Controlling anger, smiling, sharp in sight, great in caution. He does not act ignorantly, and if acted upon ignorantly, he forbears. He is not stingy, and if stingy upon, he is patient. He uses intellect, so he is bashful and content, therefore self-sufficient. His bashfulness overcomes his lust, his affection overcomes his envy, and his pardon overcomes his malice.

He does not speak except with correctness, nor wears except moderation. His walk is humility, submissive to his Lord in obedience, pleased with Him in all states. His intention is pure, his actions contain no fraud or deception. His gaze is a lesson, his silence is thought, his speech is wisdom. Advising, charitable, brotherly, advising in secret and public.

He does not forsake his brother, nor backbite him, nor plot against him. He does not despair over what is lost, nor grieve over what befalls him. He does not hope for what is not permissible, nor fails in difficulty, nor is arrogant in prosperity. He blends forbearance with knowledge, and intellect with patience. You see his laziness far, his activity near, his hope little, his slip rare.

Expectant of his term, his heart is humble, remembering his Lord. His self is content, his ignorance is negated. His affair is easy, he grieves for his sin, his lust is dead, his anger is suppressed, his character is clear, his neighbor is safe from him, his arrogance is weak. He is content with what is decreed for him, his patience is firm, his affair is decisive, his remembrance is abundant.

He mixes with people to learn, remains silent to be safe, asks to understand, and trades to gain. He does not listen to news to misuse it, nor speaks to be arrogant over others. His self is in hardship, and people are at rest from him. He exhausts himself for his Hereafter, so he rests people from himself. If attacked, he is patient until Allah avenges him. His distance from those he distances from is out of hatred and purity, and his closeness to those he approaches is out of softness and mercy. His distance is not arrogance or greatness, nor is his closeness deception or trickery. Rather, he follows those before him from the people of good, so he is an Imam for those after him from the people of righteousness.

He said: So Hammam cried out a cry, then fell unconscious. The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: 'By Allah, I was afraid of it for him.' And he said: 'This is what the delivered admonition does to its people.' A man said to him: 'What is the matter with you, O Commander of the Faithful?' He said: 'For every term there is a limit it does not exceed, and a cause it does not surpass. Wait, do not exceed, for Satan has blown upon your tongue.'
ai.seo_question: What are the spiritual and ethical characteristics of a true believer according to Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated by Hammam al-‘Abid, is a cornerstone of Shia ethical theology, often cited alongside the famous 'Description of the Believer' in Surah Al-Imran, to define the ideal spiritual and social conduct of a Shi'a. It emphasizes the believer's internal discipline (self-accounting and humility) and external justice, reflecting the Shia emphasis on *Adab* (etiquette) and *Haqq al-Nas* (rights of people) as integral to faith. The narrative context highlights the transformative power of this dense, rhythmic description, which overwhelmed Hammam, illustrating the depth of the Imam's teaching.
